evidence_candidates.claim: The AI incident response plan is scoped to AI systems, including LLM, RAG and agentic architectures, and identifies impact reduction, sensitive-data protection, evidence preservation, root-cause analysis, secure restoration and baseline telemetry as planning objectives or elements.
qualifiers: This is incident-response guidance; it does not itself establish a legal obligation.

evidence_candidates.claim: The framework assigns foundational robustness, safety alignment and inference-infrastructure security to providers, while application developers and end organisations manage prompt/context controls, application filtering, compliance monitoring and incident detection.
qualifiers: The document presents a shared-responsibility model; the listed duties are not binding requirements of the framework.

evidence_candidates.claim: The CSF mapping proposes contractually defining third-party responsibilities such as model vendors and SaaS orchestration, inventorying external connectors and data sources, and correlating provider, API and tool-execution telemetry for AI incident response.
qualifiers: The page is a framework mapping and recommendation set, not a contract or legal instrument.

evidence_candidates.claim: The shared-responsibility framework identifies vendor complexity, failed handoffs, incident-response ownership gaps and shadow AI as risks when model providers, cloud platforms, agent frameworks and application developers are connected through isolated contracts.
qualifiers: The passage describes governance pain points and does not establish liability or an obligation.

evidence_candidates.claim: The document states that it is primarily an accountability framework, complements other control frameworks, and that its referenced compliance controls illustrate accountability rather than constitute requirements of the shared-responsibility framework itself.
qualifiers: This explicit limitation prevents treating the framework examples as obligations.

evidence_candidates.claim: The framework maps evidence categories and accountable layers to artifacts such as model cards, SBOMs, API specifications, audit logs, telemetry, pen-test and red-team reports, SOC 2 attestations, dataset cards and data lineage.
qualifiers: These are proposed evidence categories and examples, not verified attestations for any provider.

evidence_candidates.claim: The agentic-AI governance framework targets organisations developing agents in-house or using third-party agentic solutions and proposes bounding action scope, limiting tools and external-system access, identity management, access controls, human checkpoints, testing and continuous monitoring.
qualifiers: The source describes emerging best practices and uses should/could language.

evidence_candidates.claim: The risk assessment treats use of externally provided or operated agents as a distinct factor because organisational visibility and control over operations and data processing may be limited; threat modelling is described as a way to identify memory poisoning, tool misuse and privilege compromise.
qualifiers: The passage supports due-diligence and risk-scoping questions; it does not assert a vendor duty.

evidence_candidates.claim: The framework recommends least-privilege access to tools and data, pre-deployment testing of task execution, policy adherence and tool-use accuracy, gradual rollout with real-time monitoring, and lifecycle change management with version control for agentic systems.
qualifiers: Recommendations are source guidance and require audit before synthesis.

evidence_candidates.claim: The Agentic IAM paper proposes treating agents as first-class identities, avoiding standing privilege, separating agent and on-behalf-of rights, binding higher-assurance identities to signed code/model manifests, enforcing authentication and authorization at every hop and preserving immutable lineage logs.
qualifiers: The paper uses MUST/SHOULD as framework language; it is not a reviewed binding source.

evidence_candidates.claim: For unknown or third-party agents, the paper describes registry-based or claims-based patterns and recommends verifiable, time-bound credentials with conservative default policies such as read-only or restricted scopes.
qualifiers: This is proposed Agentic IAM guidance, not provider assurance.

evidence_candidates.claim: At web origins, APIs, CDNs and other enforcement layers, the paper distinguishes registry-based from claims-based agent trust; it proposes tenant isolation and explicit, signed, scope- and lifetime-bounded authorization for cross-tenant delegation with tenant-isolated audit logs.
qualifiers: The passage is an interoperability and control pattern, not a contract obligation.

evidence_candidates.claim: The MCP threat model identifies identity spoofing, tool and full-schema poisoning, resource-content poisoning, typosquatting and confusion as MCP-specific threats; tool metadata from unvetted servers is treated as untrusted and transitive server calls can expand the attack surface.
qualifiers: Threat descriptions and examples do not create obligations.

evidence_candidates.claim: MCP control guidance proposes traceability from end user or initiating agent through intermediate servers to tools and services, least-privilege server operation, standard identity providers, token exchange, short-lived tokens, scope reduction and fine-grained authorization.
qualifiers: The guidance is a technical recommendation set; no binding status is asserted.

evidence_candidates.claim: MCP lifecycle guidance calls for code-signature verification, private repositories with scanning and approval workflows, dependency analysis and pinning, SBOM tracking, reproducible builds, approved-server allow-lists, centralized inventory, shadow-server discovery, staged updates and rollback capability.
qualifiers: The source uses mandatory framework wording, but it is not a reviewed BINDING source; retain as a candidate recommendation pending audit.

evidence_candidates.claim: The defender roadmap says AI risk assessment should examine model lineage and supply-chain dependencies, and that vendor evaluation should ask about open-source model versioning, incident response for harmful outputs and model-card documentation.
qualifiers: This is practical guidance; questions about a vendor do not prove the vendor's controls.

evidence_candidates.claim: The paper proposes granular model-endpoint authentication, dynamic authorization based on data sensitivity and decision impact, service-to-service authentication, and privilege tiers for AI agents; defensive AI tools should receive isolation, strict access controls and continuous monitoring.
qualifiers: The source explicitly frames these as defender guidance and examples.

evidence_candidates.claim: The AI supply-chain paper frames risks across data, models, software, infrastructure, applications and deployment, including data poisoning, compromised packages and runtime manipulation, and describes supply-chain security as spanning the AI lifecycle.
qualifiers: The executive summary is descriptive guidance, not a legal requirement.

evidence_candidates.claim: The source recommends preserving data-source versions, origins, attributes, checksums/content hashes, usage statistics and preprocessing transformations as data provenance information.
qualifiers: The recommendation supports provenance and due-diligence evidence; it does not certify any dataset or provider.

evidence_candidates.claim: For managed AI services operated by third-party providers, the source identifies visibility gaps at contractual boundaries and recommends provider security assessments, detailed security SLAs, continuous monitoring, verification mechanisms and documentation of certifications, audit reports and control mappings.
qualifiers: The source describes a managed-service risk model; no provider claim is verified here.

evidence_candidates.claim: The model-signing paper distinguishes integrity claims, provenance claims and generic property claims, with cryptographic signatures binding claims to an attesting identity and supporting traceability across AI supply-chain artifacts.
qualifiers: The source proposes a trust mechanism; it does not establish that a particular artifact or producer is trusted.

evidence_candidates.claim: The paper assigns model producers signature generation for each produced or transformed artifact and model consumers verification of attestations, including authentication of the signer identity and validation of signed information against deployment policy.
qualifiers: These are proposed producer/consumer practices, not binding obligations.

evidence_candidates.claim: The source links model signing to provenance, model validation, bias testing, performance monitoring and compliance, and describes standards and automated validation as means to verify signatures and attestations across organisational boundaries.
qualifiers: The passage is a standards and implementation recommendation; no legal status is inferred.
